newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Sao Paulo businessmen cautiously upbeat -- poll.
newsitem.headline: Sao Paulo businessmen cautiously upbeat -- poll.

text.p: Sao Paulo state businessmen are cautious but encouraged by Brazil's economic growth prospects this year and will keep a close eye on the progress of much-needed constitutional reforms, a survey said.
"Our study found businessmen moderately optimistic about Brazil," said Carlos Eduardo Moreira Ferreira, president of Sao Paulo State Industry Federation (FIESP), which polled 1,016 businessmen.
Roughly 40 percent of those polled said the country would post inflation of between eight percent and 10 percent in 1997, with economic growth of between three percent and four percent.

Ferreira said approval of constitutional reforms, which aim to slash government spending and reduce the fiscal deficit, would guarantee sustained economic growth without the threat of higher inflation.
The reform proposals have been stuck in Congress for months, with lawmakers' attention distracted by municipal elections and a controversial bill that would allow presidential re-election.
Congress, which resumed work this week after the Carnival holiday, was expected to start voting on the reforms in the next few weeks.
Despite delays in approving the reforms, the poll showed that 52 percent of the businessmen surveyed expected first half sales this year to be higher than in the same period in 1996.
Almost 30 percent of the businessmen forecast sales to grow by up to 11 percent in 1997, it added.

More than 60 percent of businessmen polled said their performance in 1997 would be good, while five percent said it would be excellent. Thirty-one percent said performance would be moderate and only three percent said it would be worse, the survey said.
Some 51 percent of those polled were not planning to cut jobs this year, while 39 percent said they would cut staff.
Ferreira said roughly 90 percent of the firms will be investing to modernize their plants or eliminate production bottlenecks this year.
"This shows that job cuts will not be as numerous as they were in 1996," said Horacio Lafer Piva, head of Fiesp's research department.
The survey also showed that 55 percent of businessmen believe their products are competitive with imports, while 22 percent said their products would not be able to compete with imports.
